UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.
)
Docket No. ER26-3515-000
PROTEST OF THE ELECTRIC POWER SUPPLY ASSOCIATION 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal 
Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or the “Commission”),1 the Electric Power 
Supply Association (“EPSA”)2 submits this protest to the August 13, 2026, filing by PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) proposing to establish Interim Resource Adequacy 
Service (“IRAS”).3  EPSA’s members stand ready to supply the power necessary to 
meet surging demand in PJM and to support the development of data centers in the 
region.  Regrettably, however, PJM’s IRAS proposal4 will hinder, rather than advance, 
those goals and undermine reliability and competition in the PJM footprint.  While the 
IRAS proposal suffers from numerous legal defects, any number of which would, on

2

U.S.  EPSA members provide reliable and competitively priced electricity from environmentally 
responsible facilities using a diverse mix of fuels and technologies.  EPSA seeks to bring the 
benefits of competition to all power customers.  This filing represents the position of EPSA as an 
organization, but not necessarily the views of any particular member with respect to any issue.  
EPSA has separately moved to intervene in this proceeding.  See (doc-less) Motion to Intervene 
of the Electric Power Supply Association, Docket No. ER26-3515-000 (filed Aug. 14, 2026).

Proposal of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. to Establish Interim Resource Adequacy

(filed Aug. 13, 2026) (the “August 13 Filing”).  Capitalized terms not defined herein have the 
meaning set forth in the August 13 Filing or, if not therein defined, the Reliability Assurance 
Agreement Among Load Serving Entities (the “RAA”) and the PJM Open Access Transmission 
Tariff (the “Tariff”), as applicable.

The August 13 Filing also proposes to establish a Large Load Registry.  EPSA does not 
object to this aspect of the August 13 Filing.

2 
their own, compel rejection of that proposal, EPSA is particularly concerned about the 
blatantly discriminatory element of the IRAS proposal that would only allow new 
capacity resources (referred to as “Bring Your Own New Capacity” or “BYONC”) to be 
used to serve New Large Loads without interruption.  This aspect of PJM’s proposal is 
not only legally defective but also represents the type of market design choice that 
undermines confidence in PJM and the durability of its market structures, precisely at a 
time when PJM needs to be rebuilding investor confidence for the long-term benefit of 
consumers.   
Fortunately, there are alternatives, including one described below, to the flawed 
approach put forth by PJM that would address the policy concerns underlying the IRAS 
proposal.  And importantly, the alternative approach described below avoids the serious 
harm to the Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) construct and the undermining of its ability 
to ensure reliability and the illegal discrimination against existing resources that would 
result from the IRAS proposal. 
I. 
PROTEST 
As detailed herein and in the affidavit of Paul M. Sotkiewicz, Ph.D., provided as 
Attachment A hereto (the “Sotkiewicz Affidavit”), the IRAS proposal set forth in the 
August 13 Filing is unduly discriminatory and preferential and otherwise unlawful and 
must therefore be rejected in its entirety.   
A. 
PJM’s BYONC Requirement for New Large Loads is Unduly 
Preferential and Discriminatory, and Otherwise Unlawful under 
Section 205 of the FPA 
The IRAS proposal and, in particular, the BYONC requirement, would, by design, 
drive a wedge between new and existing load, and between new and existing capacity

3 
resources in the RPM market.  Under PJM’s IRAS proposal, a New Large Load will be 
“eligible to provide IRAS as [an] Eligible New Large Load,” unless it has obtained 
BYONC sufficient to meet its capacity needs.5  While PJM attempts to soft pedal the 
nature of its proposal by describing these new loads as “eligible” to provide the new 
“service” (IRAS), Eligible New Large Loads will, in fact, be required to provide IRAS, 
and the “service” they will be providing is to be put at the front of the line for 
curtailment.6  The only way a New Large Load can avoid becoming “eligible” is to 
contract for sufficient new capacity (i.e., BYONC) in advance.7  On its face, this 
restriction unduly discriminates against existing resources and New Large Loads and 
grants an undue preference to new resources and loads other than New Large Loads, 
in direct contravention of the FPA.8  Equally importantly, and as explained by Dr. 
 
5  
August 13 Filing, Transmittal Letter at 36. 
6  
See id., Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, § IV(a) (“All Eligible New Large Loads shall 
be available to be requested to provide Interim Resource Adequacy Service by [PJM].”). 
7  
This requirement suggests that PJM is seeking to dictate the terms of retail sales that 
are the exclusive provenance of the states under the FPA.  See 16 U.S.C. § 824(b); FERC v. 
Electric Power Supply Ass’n, 577 U.S. 260, 279-80 (2016) (stating that the FPA “reserv[es] 
regulatory authority over retail sales (as well as intrastate wholesale sales) to the States,” such 
that “FERC cannot take an action transgressing that limit no matter how direct, or dramatic, its 
impact on wholesale rates,” and that any rule that “specifies terms of sale at retail . . . is a job for 
the States alone”).  Critically, however, even assuming that the Commission has the authority to 
approve a new PJM “service” that seeks to dictate the purchasing practices of customers and 
curtailment priorities of load-serving entities (“LSEs”), the IRAS proposal is being implemented 
in a way that is unduly preferential to new generation and unduly discriminatory to existing 
generation as described herein. 
8  
See 16 U.S.C. § 824d(b) (2024); 16 U.S.C. § 824e(a) (2024).  See also, e.g., FPC v. 
Conway Corp., 426 U.S. 271, 277 (1976) (“Section 205(b) forbids the maintenance of any 
‘unreasonable difference in rates’ or service ‘with respect to any . . . sale subject to the 
jurisdiction of the Commission.’” (quoting 16 U.S.C. § 824d(b))); Wisconsin Pub. Power, Inc. v. 
FERC, 493 F.3d 239, 246 (D.C. Cir. 2007) (“Section 205 . . . prohibits undue discrimination in 
rates, charges, or terms of service.” (citation omitted)).

4 
Sotkiewicz, the unlawful discrimination will not help achieve PJM’s goals and will 
instead result in higher costs for all consumers and lower reliability over the long term.9 
To begin, PJM’s distinctions between New Large Loads and other loads are 
utterly arbitrary and highly discriminatory.  PJM has articulated no valid reason why a 
new 49.9 MW load will not be subject to IRAS, while load that crosses the 50 MW 
threshold set by PJM must obtain new capacity.  Nor has it explained why load that 
goes into service on May 31, 2027, should be treated differently from load that goes into 
service just one day later, on June 1, 2027, or why the load that enters service after 
June 1, 2027, should be considered “new” when it was presumably being developed for 
years.  This arbitrary deadline is impossible to reconcile with PJM’s statement that pre-
existing commercial arrangements will not be impacted.  In fact, the arbitrary nature of 
PJM’s proposal is highlighted by its statement that “the relevant in-service date for a 
Large Load to qualify as New Large Load will fluctuate based on whether or not IRAS is 
needed . . . .”10  That is, new load coming into service in one year could be subject to 
IRAS, while load that comes into service a year later would not, even though any 
capacity shortfall or surplus in each of those years could be the result of system 
conditions as a whole, rather than being solely attributable to new load.  PJM’s proposal 
to single out loads arbitrarily defined as New Large Loads violates not only the 
prohibition against undue discrimination in Section 205(b) of the FPA11 but also the

requirements of Section 202(g)(3)(B) of the FPA.12  The latter provision expressly 
provides that in the case of “any anticipated shortage of electric energy or capacity 
which would affect [a public] utility’s capability of serving its wholesale customers,”13 the 
public utility must accommodate such shortage in a manner that assures that “all 
persons served directly or indirectly by such public utility will be treated, without undue 
prejudice or disadvantage.”14 
The unlawfully preferential and discriminatory treatment under the IRAS proposal 
is not limited to load but, because of the BYONC aspect of the IRAS proposal, extends 
to capacity resources.  The RPM market is designed to procure one product:  Unforced 
Capacity (“UCAP”).  As PJM itself explains:

underlying physical resource that supports a Capacity 
Resource.  RPM Auctions clear MW of UCAP; that is the 
traded product.15 
Similarly, the Commission has described RPM as procuring “a single capacity product,”16 
whereby there are “the same expectations for all Capacity Performance Resources 
without regard to technology type.”17  Indeed, RPM is premised on an understanding of

resources, regardless of their vintage.18  Accordingly, since its inception, the RPM market 
has been designed to “permit generation, demand response, and transmission a 
reasonable opportunity to compete in solving reliability concerns,”19 whereby each Base 
Residual Auction (“BRA”) was intentionally held sufficiently in advance to “allow new entry 
by resources to compete with existing capacity.”20  The Commission has therefore 
rejected calls for rules that would favor existing resources over future resources, given 
that “the two resources are similarly situated in their ability to meet PJM's resource 
adequacy needs during a given Delivery Year”21 and likewise rejected a PJM proposal 
that would have “grant[ed] more favorable treatment to resources the earlier they enter 
the capacity market.”22  The Commission also rejected a proposal that would have 
“provide[d] additional payments to new generators but not to existing generators,” finding 
that this would not “support our objective of achieving an efficient market overall” and 
would “not treat all capacity suppliers equally.”23  Instead, the Commission made clear 
that “[i]n a competitive market, all suppliers will be paid the same price.”24

Nonetheless, PJM now proposes to exclude existing resources from satisfying 
the capacity needs of New Large Load.25  Under PJM’s proposal, even if a New Large 
Load has purchased sufficient existing capacity to meet its needs, PJM would treat the 
New Large Load as “eligible” (meaning: “required”) to provide IRAS (meaning: first to be 
curtailed after non-firm transmission and before demand response).  The effect of this 
requirement will be to force New Large Loads to purchase capacity only from new 
resources, such that “one set of resources will be effectively barred from selling capacity 
to New Large Loads while the other will have that opportunity, despite both providing the 
exact same service.”26  To make matters worse, because PJM proposes to exclude New 
Large Loads that do not have sufficient BYONC from its Variable Resource 
Requirement (“VRR”) Curve, the VRR Curve will not reflect “the true supply-demand 
balance in the RPM market,” which will “all other things equal, . . . result in differential 
pricing between Existing Capacity Resources and BYONC Resources.”27  As Dr. 
Sotkiewicz observes, there is no reliability justification for this exclusion.28  This means 
that existing resources “will presumably face lower prices and will never get the benefit 
of price formation that will price in new entry in the market as it is needed.”29  
Accordingly, the BYONC requirement can be expected to result in lower rates for

substantially similar service works an unlawful discrimination.”30 
Of course, because RPM only procures “a single capacity product,”31 existing 
resources are no less capable of meeting the capacity needs of New Large Loads than 
new resources.  That is, PJM could easily have designed its IRAS proposal to require 
New Large Loads to “Bring Your Own Capacity,” rather than “Bring Your Own New 
Capacity.”  PJM’s decision not to do so appears to stem from a misplaced belief that 
existing load has some preferential right to the capacity provided by existing resources, 
such that new load must be served with new capacity.  But this makes no sense in the 
context of PJM’s RPM market, which only provides year-to-year compensation.  Indeed, 
the notion that existing loads enjoy some sort of preferential right to capacity from 
existing resources is contrary to the fundamental economic principles underlying 
commodity markets32 and ignores the fact that RPM was designed to allow new and 
existing resources to compete for the benefit of consumers.33  In fact, the unduly 
preferential treatment of new resources and undue discrimination against existing

PJM nonetheless attempts to rationalize the BYONC requirement by claiming 
that: 
[t]his aspect of the IRAS framework is consistent with the 
Ratepayer Protection Pledge introduced in March 2026 and 
recently expanded in July 2026, which recognizes that New 
Large Loads “will voluntarily negotiate new, separate rate 
structures with their utilities and relevant State governments 
wherever they build data centers.”35 
While the goals and requirements of the Ratepayer Protection Pledge are laudable, the 
Ratepayer Protection Pledge in no way justifies or necessitates PJM’s BYONC 
requirement.  As an initial matter, by its terms, the Ratepayer Protection Pledge only 
commits the signatory companies to “voluntarily negotiate new, separate rate structures 
with their utilities and relevant State governments . . . .”36  While the signatory companies 
are free to voluntarily negotiate purchases of capacity only from new resources in 
furtherance of this commitment, there is nothing in the pledge that even remotely 
suggests that PJM should be allowed to refuse firm service to signatories, much less to 
non-signatories, or that otherwise contemplates anything like the IRAS proposal.  As PJM 
acknowledges, the signatory companies are only “[a] representative class of the[] New

Large Loads are signatories to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge,”37 and even if this 
representative class could somehow be understood to have bound all New Large Loads 
(and they cannot be), the Ratepayer Protection Pledge provides no legal basis for fulfilling 
New Large Loads’ commitments at the expense of existing resources, as PJM’s IRAS 
proposal would do.38 
More fundamentally, the Ratepayer Protection Pledge does not and cannot 
rewrite the FPA or override the FPA’s prohibition against unduly discriminatory or 
preferential rates and rate classifications.  Accordingly, even if the Ratepayer Protection 
Pledge could be reimagined as supporting PJM’s IRAS proposal, the Commission 
would still be statutorily bound to reject that proposal. 
B. 
The Sotkiewicz Affidavit Identifies Other Unjust, Unreasonable, and 
Unduly Preferential and Discriminatory Aspects of the IRAS Proposal 
As discussed above, the IRAS proposal clearly results in undue discrimination 
against existing resources and New Large Loads and undue preference in favor of new 
resources and existing loads and new loads other than New Large Loads.  As Dr. 
Sotkiewicz explains in detail, however, the discrimination inherent in the IRAS proposal 
extends beyond the eligibility requirements and has numerous unjust, unreasonable and 
unduly discriminatory side effects. 
First, the IRAS proposal grants BYONC resources unduly preferential treatment 
with respect to Effective Load Carrying Capability (“ELCC”) accreditation.  Under PJM’s

auctions, where such Accredited UCAP may vary from year to year based on each 
resource’s performance as well as system conditions.39  By contrast, the August 13 
Filing proposes to shelter BYONC resources from ELCC variability and lets them lock-in 
the Accredited UCAP for the RPM Auction in which they first clear.40  Similarly, New 
Large Load that has contracted with BYONC also benefits from this unduly preferential 
treatment, given that it is “insulated from ELCC volatility while other loads must face the 
market implications of that year-to-year volatility.”41  The Commission previously 
rejected a similar proposal that would have “discriminate[d] between resources in a 
class based on vintage . . . .”42  It is vital that the Commission likewise reject this 
vintaging proposal, because the proposed preferential treatment of BYONC will likely to 
result in its capacity contribution being overstated in RPM Auctions, which will “further 
erode[] the fidelity of the RPM BRA or IA price signal . . . .”43  This will undermine RPM’s 
ability to maintain reliability, because it will “mask[] potential resource adequacy 
shortfalls in the future and send[] price signals that no new entry is needed.”44  
Second, the IRAS proposal also unduly discriminates against BYONC resources 
through 10-year offer requirements, which reflect unsupported assumptions regarding

sufficient to completely cover the going forward costs of the BYONC.47  Such an 
assumption is unsupported, and PJM fails to explain why BYONC should be subject to a 
price-taker obligation when other contracted resources are not.  Moreover, while PJM 
proposes to lift these offer requirements if IRAS is not needed for three consecutive 
years, PJM fails to explain why there is no exemption if, for example, the underlying 
BYONC contract is no longer in effect (e.g., the New Large Load fails to materialize or 
breaches the contract). 
Third, PJM also proposes not to apply IRAS to load within the service area of

alternative.  That is, FRR Entities may “potentially use existing resources to meet New 
Large Loads while other LSEs can only use existing resources to serve existing 
loads.”48  While the BYONC requirement is, as discussed in detail above, unduly 
preferential and discriminatory and must be rejected, it makes no sense for PJM to 
apply this requirement only in some areas and not others.

“[n]o other loads on the PJM system that are curtailed, including those voluntarily doing 
so as Economic Demand Response or for peak load shaving purposes, are 
compensated in the same manner for energy reductions as Eligible New Large Loads, 
though the load reductions will have the same reliability benefit.”51 
C. 
The IRAS Proposal Should be Rejected in Its Entirety 
To be clear, EPSA understands and appreciates the need for PJM to make 
market changes to address the capacity shortfall and reliability concerns in its region.  
But the solution to these problems cannot be to violate the FPA and embed undue 
discrimination in PJM’s market rules.  Even aside from being forbidden by the FPA, such 
discriminatory treatment simply slaps a band-aid on the problem while potentially 
making the underlying wound worse.  Indeed, Dr. Sotkiewicz explains that the incentives 
created by IRAS may aggravate the problems that are already plaguing the region.52  As 
has been made clear by PJM’s experiences over the last few years, consumers are the 
ones that will be ultimately harmed if PJM fails to ensure that existing resources are 
treated fairly.  FTI Consulting recently cautioned that, while “[d]iscriminatory capacity 
markets can in some circumstances result in short-run reductions in consumer

D. 
There Are Alternatives Available to PJM and the Commission that 
Would Preserve the Integrity of the RPM Construct While Protecting 
Existing Loads 
While EPSA appreciates the policy concerns that PJM is attempting to address 
through the IRAS proposal, it is well-established that “policy interests . . . cannot 
override the statute.”60  As discussed above, the IRAS proposal is inherently 
discriminatory and otherwise unlawful and must be rejected.  Importantly, however, it 
does not follow that PJM, the Commission and state regulators are powerless to protect 
other loads from the resource adequacy issues presented by new large loads, as there 
are alternative approaches to address the concerns underlying the IRAS proposal.  For 
example, PJM could require LSEs that are deficient capacity to designate load – either 
their own load or contracted demand response – that will be curtailed in the event PJM 
is in a load shed event.  This requirement will achieve the same goals as the IRAS 
proposal:  generation-deficient LSEs will have an incentive to contract for capacity, 
including new capacity, and load shed designations can be structured to protect

A. Commodity Markets Trade Fungible Commodities 
16. 
A commodity is fungible when it can be replaced with an identical commodity, regardless 
of source of the original or replacement commodity.13 
 
13 See https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/fungible.

7 
 
17. 
Commodity fungibility is a core requirement for markets to reach efficient outcomes as the 
fungibility of the commodity allows buyers and sellers to find suitable, creditworthy 
counterparties with whom to transact on a bilateral basis, and to understand what is being 
transacted in centralized auction frameworks. 
18. 
Commodity fungibility gives a party who has sold a commodity the option to replace that 
commodity on a one-for-one basis should it fail to deliver on its original commitment, and 
the purchasing counterparty is assured that what it receives is what it paid for. In this sense, 
commodity fungibility helps provide liquidity, which is the ability to quickly buy or sell 
the underlying commodity, at going market prices without incurring significant transaction 
costs such as the cost for searching for the “appropriate counterparty” to meet a specific 
one-of-a-kind requirement.
